name: Victor Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a team of five demand planners at the head office of a supermarket chain. We forecast how much chilled food each store needs, so yoghurt, ready meals, salads, the stuff that goes off in four days. My morning is a call with the buyers, then I check the orders the system suggests and argue about the ones that look wrong. After lunch it's mostly one-to-ones with my planners and fixing whatever went sideways with the weather.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The weather, honestly. One hot weekend and every store runs out of salad, and the stores blame us. I've only been leading the team a year, and two of my planners know more than I do, which is humbling. I use the AI chat thing now and then to tidy up my emails, but I don't let it near the numbers yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that the tools are fine but someone still has to know what a bank holiday does to hummus sales. At work I'd be the boring middle voice in the room. Online I don't post much, maybe a joke about all the money spent on AI consultants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I've got time to get good at this, which I need. I'm not the best planner on my team, and if nothing changes I can grow into the job. My savings are in index funds my uncle talked me into, so I'm not lying awake about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and take the forecasting course the company offers in spring. I'd probably let the AI write the first draft of my weekly summary, because that saves me an hour and nobody reads it closely anyway. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about your life worrying you, even in that calmer picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, a bit. I'm on good pay but rent in the city keeps climbing, and my flatmate Jonas is moving out next year. That's a real cost for me whatever happens with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI change how your team works at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, just the hour on Friday. The AI writes my weekly summary, I fix the bits where it gets the yoghurt numbers wrong, and I go home on time.

say: I'd say someone still has to know what a **bank holiday** does to sales.
I'd joke about the money spent on **AI consultants**.
think: A calm world gives me **time to get good** at the job.
My **index funds** mean money isn't keeping me up.
do: Take the company's **forecasting course** in spring.
Let AI draft the **weekly summary** to save an hour.
Budget for higher **rent** once my flatmate moves out.
S0.quote: The AI writes my weekly summary, I fix the bits where it gets the yoghurt numbers wrong, and I go home on time.
fieldNote: He knows he's **not the best planner** on his own team and wants time to catch up.
His only real pressure is **rising rent** when his flatmate leaves.
He uses AI for **small chores** but keeps it away from the numbers.

steps.text: Take the company's forecasting course in spring
Let the AI draft the Friday weekly summary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one's real, because buying and planning are right there on the list. I'd say it at work too, carefully, that we should decide together how to use it instead of just having it dropped on us. Online I'd share stuff about taxing the companies that save the most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my team of five becomes two planners and a dashboard. The order suggestions are already decent, and a better system would beat my weaker planners and probably me. The person who sits between the planners and the buyers is the first job they'd fold into something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the forecasting AI properly now, not just for emails, so I'm the one who understands it. I'd ask for a seat on whatever group picks the new system. And I'd move more of my pay into savings, maybe an extra 300 a month, in case I need a gap between jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say. Not falling apart, but it's there when I wake up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'folded into something else' look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my own role disappears into the buyer team, and the buyers start doing planning themselves with the software. My job is basically translating between planners and buyers, and the new software speaks both languages without needing me in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be learning the system that might replace your team. Does that sit right with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I would, because I'd be the one deciding who learns it and who gets left behind. Getting better at the tool is the only way I get a say.

say: I'd say this one's **real**, because planning and buying are on the list.
I'd push for staff to **decide together** how the tools get used.
Online I'd share ideas about **taxing** the biggest savers.
think: My team of five shrinks to **two planners** and a dashboard.
The **go-between** role is the first to get folded away.
do: Learn the **forecasting AI** properly, not just for emails.
Ask for a **seat** on the group choosing the system.
Save an **extra 300** a month for a gap between jobs.
feel: **Anxious**, a worry that's there when he wakes up.
S1.quote: My job is basically translating between planners and buyers, and the new software speaks both languages without needing me in the middle.
fieldNote: He sees his job as **translation** between teams, which software could do.
He learns the tool to keep **a say**, even knowing it may replace his team.
His public line is cautious; privately he expects **his role to vanish**.

steps.text: Learn the forecasting AI on real chilled-food orders
Ask for a seat on the group choosing the new system
Move an extra 300 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments, fast: a tax on the savings and some kind of basic income, at least for a while. I'd sign every petition and probably go to a march. At work I'd say it's not our fault, and the company owes people time and money to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm done in head office by 2029. Forecasting is pure thinking work, and AGI does it better than the whole team. The only part of the supermarket that keeps people for a few years is the hands-on side, the depots and stores, until the robots come about three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd try to move to a depot operations role, managing the night shift loading lorries, because that's hands-on for a while. I'd cut back hard, move somewhere cheaper when Jonas leaves, and keep my index funds untouched. And I'd vote and campaign for whoever takes the basic income idea seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A bit dizzy, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving to the depot is a hands-on job. Do the three years before robots really help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years in a depot gives me a wage and time to think, but it's borrowed time. A night shift in a depot buys me three years, and then the robots that load the lorries arrive and I'm back where I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you moved somewhere cheaper, where would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a small room, maybe back near my parents in the town I grew up in. My mum would like that more than me.

say: I'd demand a **tax** on savings and some kind of **basic income**.
I'd tell the company it **owes people** time and money.
think: Only the **depots and stores** keep people for a few years.
do: Apply for a **night depot** manager role in the first year.
Move somewhere **cheaper** when the flatmate leaves.
S2.quote: A night shift in a depot buys me three years, and then the robots that load the lorries arrive and I'm back where I started.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** deliberately, moving from desk planning into a depot.
He sees the depot move as **borrowed time**, not a real answer.
His politics turn practical: **basic income** and tax, not slowing the tech.

steps.text: Apply for a night-shift depot manager role in the first year
Rent a cheaper room when Jonas moves out
Campaign for candidates who back a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so let's use it. I'd push for a proper retraining scheme with the unions and the company at the table. With friends I'd say we're all in the same boat, which helps a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I've got about four good years left in planning, and I'm using them to get out of the line of fire. I'd still be young, 32 at the end, and I have money behind me. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year really learning the AI side and offer to run the team that checks its forecasts, because someone signs them off for a while. Then I'd look at a course in supply chain for the public side, like hospital supplies, where I think they'll move slower. I'd keep the extra savings going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the two-year one. I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hospital supplies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hospitals and councils change slowly, and I'd rather work for something public anyway. Hospitals change slower than supermarkets, so I'd rather spend my last planning years keeping wards stocked than keeping yoghurt on shelves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager say if you left?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager Fiona would probably cheer me on and then quietly be glad there's one fewer head to cut. I don't hate her for that.

say: I'd call five years a **warning** we should use.
I'd push for **retraining** with unions and the company together.
think: Planning has about **four good years** left for me.
Being young with **money behind me** helps a lot.
do: Learn the AI side and offer to run **forecast checking**.
Take a **supply chain course** aimed at hospital supplies.
Keep the **extra savings** going each month.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to breathe this time.
S3.quote: Hospitals change slower than supermarkets, so I'd rather spend my last planning years keeping wards stocked than keeping yoghurt on shelves.
fieldNote: Five years turns his plan from escape into a **staged move**.
He chooses **public sector** work for both pace and values.
He understands his manager's **mixed motives** without resentment.

steps.text: Offer to run the team that checks the AI's forecasts
Enrol in a supply chain course for hospital supplies
Keep the extra 300 a month going into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to make this good for people, and if we waste it, that's on politicians. I'd talk about a shorter working week a lot. I'd probably bore my friends with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when it arrives, so this is my whole career's middle. Ten years is enough to build a second skill, but I don't think there's a planning job left at the end of it. I'm less scared and more sort of resigned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in planning for three or four years and get really good with the AI tools while they still need people to check them. Meanwhile I'd study something slow to automate, maybe procurement for public health, part-time. I'd keep buying index funds every month, because if machines do the work, owning a slice of the companies matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I think. A slower, duller version of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think planning will still exist for you at the end of those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and I don't love saying that. Ten years only gives me time to plan around losing the planning job, and that feels a bit sad for something I trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour public support, but you're also buying shares. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a bit funny, because I'm the progressive guy saying share the wealth, and then I'm buying shares. I'd say both are true. If nobody shares, I'd rather not be the one with nothing.

say: I'd say a decade is time to make this **good for people**.
I'd talk endlessly about a **shorter working week**.
think: He'd be **37** when it arrives, in the middle of his career.
He doesn't expect a **planning job** left at the end.
do: Stay in planning **three or four years** and master the checking tools.
feel: **Anxious** in a slower, duller way, close to resignation.
S4.quote: Ten years only gives me time to plan around losing the planning job, and that feels a bit sad for something I trained for.
fieldNote: He holds two views at once: **share the wealth** and own shares himself.
Ten years changes the **pace** of his plan, not where it ends.
He's sad about losing work he **trained for**, not scared of poverty.

steps.text: Stay in planning for three years and master the AI tools
Keep buying index funds every month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm young and I've got savings, but I'd be one of millions of planners and analysts all looking for the same depot jobs. The scary part isn't losing my job, it's losing my job in the same month as everyone else who does what I do. What would help is a basic income while people retrain, paid for by the companies that save the most.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I'd miss the people. My planners are funny, and Thursday lunch at the noodle place across the road is the best part of my week. Nobody puts that in a forecast.

headlineQuote: The scary part isn't losing my job, it's losing my job in the same month as everyone else who does what I do.
portrait: Victor is **27** and leads five demand planners for chilled food at a supermarket chain's head office.
He's still learning, admits two of his planners know more, and uses AI only **for emails** for now.
He has **index funds** behind him and lives in a shared city flat.
He leans **progressive**, wants tax and basic income, but would still learn the tools to keep a say.
As AGI gets closer he'd shift towards **depots** or **hospital supplies**, which he expects to change slower.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing his job at the same time as every other **planner**.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** while people retrain, paid for by companies saving the most.
